title: Lesson 7: When You Drift
description: You will stumble. Every Christian does. This lesson is not about guilt. It is about knowing how to turn around when you wander off the path, how to confess honestly, and how to trust the Shepherd who comes looking for you before you even know you are lost.

blocks.text: You have walked through six lessons now: what it means to follow Jesus, to be saved and baptized, to pray, to read the Bible, to be part of a church family, and to share your faith. This final lesson may be the one that holds all the others together. No matter how well you learn the foundations, there will be days when you drift. You will sin. You will wander. And when that happens, you need to know what to do next.

blocks.title: The Shepherd Who Comes Looking
blocks.text:
Jesus told a story about a shepherd who had a hundred sheep. Picture one of them wandering off, not in rebellion and not by any plan, just drifting one patch of grass at a time, until it looks up and realizes it is alone.

"What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing." (Luke 15:4-5)

Notice what the shepherd does. He does not wait for the sheep to find its way back. He does not stand at the gate shaking his head. He leaves everything and goes after the one. And when he finds it, he does not scold it. He puts it on his shoulders and carries it home, and then he calls his friends and neighbors to celebrate. Jesus finished the story this way: "Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance" (Luke 15:7).

That is the heart of God toward you. He is not waiting to punish you when you wander. He comes looking. When you drift, you do not have to find your way back alone. Turn around, and the Shepherd carries you home.
7.1 - When have you felt like the lost sheep, drifting without even realizing it?
What Repentance Really Means

Many people hear the word "repentance" and picture guilt, shame, or punishment. But the Bible paints a completely different picture. The Greek word for repentance is metanoia, and it means a change of mind that leads to a change of direction. Picture a 180-degree turn. You were walking one direction, away from God, and now you stop, turn around, and walk toward Him. Not groveling. Not earning your way back. Just turning.

Sin always promises something good around the next bend, but the road just gets darker. Repentance is the moment you stop believing that lie and turn your whole self around. And the moment you turn, you discover the Shepherd was already coming to find you.
Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord.

Did you catch that? Turning back does not lead to punishment, it leads to refreshing. Repentance is not the end of something good. It is the beginning of something better: the doorway back to peace, back to closeness with God, back to the life you were actually made for.
Confession: Keeping the Air Clear

If repentance is the big turn, confession is the daily practice that keeps your heart clean. Confession simply means agreeing with God about what happened. You stop hiding, stop excusing, and stop pretending. You just say it out loud: "Lord, I was impatient with my family. I lied about that. I chose my comfort over obedience."
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

Read that promise slowly. He is faithful, meaning He will always do it. He is just, meaning the cross already paid the price, so forgiving you is not a favor, it is a finished transaction. And He does not just forgive, He cleanses. Not halfway. All of it.

Here is what a new believer needs to understand: confession does not change your standing with God. When you trusted Jesus, you became His child forever. But unconfessed sin clouds the closeness you feel with Him. A child who disobeys a parent is still their child, but there is tension in the home until things are made right. Confession clears the air and brings you back into the warmth of the Father's presence.

blocks.title: The Way Home: Stop, Turn, Tell, Receive
content: Stop. Notice the drift. Be honest that you have wandered off the path.
Turn. Change direction and walk back toward God. "Repent therefore, and turn back" (Acts 3:19).
Tell. Confess to God what happened, by name and without excuses (1 John 1:9).
Receive. Take the forgiveness Jesus already secured at the cross. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).

blocks.text: That is the simplest version of repentance, and you can walk it in a few honest minutes, any day, anywhere. In a future course, you will learn a fuller tool called The Learning Circle that walks through this rhythm step by step.
7.2 - Is there something you have been carrying that you need to confess to God today?
Conviction Is Not Condemnation

One of the most important things to understand as a new believer is the difference between two voices. Condemnation is the voice of the enemy. It says, "You are a failure. You will never change. Give up." It drives you away from God and into shame. Conviction is the voice of the Holy Spirit. It says, "You have sinned. Come home to the Father." It draws you back to God and into grace.

The difference is the direction they push you. If what you are feeling makes you want to run from God, that is not His voice. If what you are feeling makes you want to run to God, that is the Holy Spirit doing exactly what He was sent to do.
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
7.3 - Think about a time you felt guilty. Did that feeling push you away from God or draw you toward Him?
When You Stumble, Get Back Up

You will stumble, and every Christian does. A new believer needs to know this up front, because without that honesty, failure can feel like the end of the road when it is not. What defines you is not your failures but Jesus' faithfulness. The mark of a true follower of Jesus is not perfection, it is getting back up and walking with Him again.
Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.

That is the promise. When you fall, you will rise. When you sit in darkness, the Lord Himself will be a light to you. Not because you are strong enough to recover, but because the Shepherd who left the ninety-nine is strong enough to carry you home.
Looking Back on the Journey

You have now walked through all seven lessons of the Starting in Discipleship course. You have explored what it means to follow Jesus, to be saved and baptized, to pray, to read the Bible, to be part of the church, to share your faith, and to turn back to God when you drift. These are not just topics you have studied. They are the foundations of a life that is being transformed by the grace of God.

Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit.
7.4 - As you look back on all seven lessons and the Gospel of John, what has changed in your walk with God?
Lesson 7 Review

When you drift, you do not have to find your way back alone. Repentance is not a burden. It is a gift: a turn back to a Shepherd who was already coming to find you. Stop, turn, tell God what happened, and receive the forgiveness Jesus already secured. Confession keeps the air clear, and the Holy Spirit's conviction is not condemnation. It is love drawing you home.

You have completed the Starting in Discipleship course. The next step is Growing Deep, where you will go deeper into your identity in Christ, explore the cross, and learn practical tools for walking with God through every season.

blocks.heading: Introduction to John 19, 20, and 21
blocks.intro: In John 19-21, you will read the most important events in all of human history: the crucifixion, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Take your time with these chapters, because this is the foundation that everything you have studied in this course is built on.
